topic: Primary Aldosteronism Diagnostic Confirmation and Subtype Differentiation
stem: A 43-year-old man presents with persistent hypertension. He takes amlodipine 10 mg daily and hydralazine 50 mg three times daily. His blood pressure is 158/98 mm Hg. Laboratory evaluation shows serum potassium 3.1 mEq/L, serum sodium 143 mEq/L, and serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. He was transitioned off potassium-wasting diuretics and beta-blockers, and hypokalemia was fully repleted. A morning screening test reveals: plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) 32 ng/dL (normal 3-16 ng/dL) and plasma renin activity (PRA) 0.4 ng/mL/h, yielding an aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) of 80 (positive cutoff > 20-30). Confirmatory high-sodium oral salt-loading testing demonstrates a 24-hour urine aldosterone excretion of 24 mcg/24h (normal < 12 mcg/24h), confirming autonomous primary aldosteronism. High-resolution thin-section computed tomography (CT) of the adrenal glands demonstrates a well-circumscribed 1.3-cm hypoattenuating nodule in the left adrenal gland and a normal right adrenal gland. The patient expresses a strong desire for curative surgical management. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step prior to proceeding with unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy?

options.text: Proceed directly to left laparoscopic adrenalectomy based on the definitive CT finding
options.explanation: Proceeding directly to surgery based on CT alone results in inappropriate adrenalectomy in 20-30% of patients who actually have bilateral adrenal hyperplasia or a non-functioning incidentaloma with contralateral hypersecretion.

options.text: Perform fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy of the 1.3-cm left adrenal nodule
options.explanation: Adrenal FNA cannot distinguish a benign aldosterone-producing adenoma from a non-functioning cortical adenoma or normal cortex; it risks adrenal hematoma, hypertensive crisis if pheochromocytoma is present, and tumor tract seeding.

options.text: Perform bilateral adrenal vein sampling (AVS) with ACTH stimulation to differentiate unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma from bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
options.explanation: PRIMARY ALDOSTERONISM (PA, Conn syndrome) is a leading cause of secondary hypertension. After demonstrating an elevated ARR (> 20-30 with PAC > 15 ng/dL) and confirming autonomous aldosterone production with a suppression test (oral sodium loading, IV saline infusion, or fludrocortisone suppression), SUBTYPE DIFFERENTIATION IS CRITICAL before considering curative surgical intervention. Primary aldosteronism is caused by either UNILATERAL ALDOSTERONE-PRODUCING ADENOMA (APA, ~35-40%, cured by laparoscopic adrenalectomy) or BILATERAL IDIOPATHIC ADRENAL HYPERPLASIA (IHA, ~60%, managed medically with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists). Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) is inherently unreliable for subtype classification because: (1) non-functional adrenal incidentalomas are common with advancing age (> 10% in older adults), meaning an imaged nodule may be a non-functioning bystander while the contralateral micro-nodule secretes aldosterone; and (2) APA can be microscopic and invisible on CT. Therefore, Endocrine Society guidelines designate BILATERAL ADRENAL VEIN SAMPLING (AVS) as the GOLD STANDARD to confirm lateralization of aldosterone hypersecretion before laparoscopic adrenalectomy. (Exception: patients < 35 years old with marked hypokalemia and a solitary large unilateral adenoma > 1 cm may proceed directly to surgery).

options.text: Initiate lifelong amiloride 10 mg daily without further diagnostic testing
options.explanation: In patients who are surgical candidates seeking cure, subtype differentiation with AVS is indicated; medical therapy is reserved for bilateral hyperplasia or non-surgical candidates.

options.text: Obtain a 24-hour urine collection for fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines
options.explanation: The patient has biochemically proven autonomous hyperaldosteronism (high PAC/PRA ratio and unsuppressed urinary aldosterone); pheochromocytoma is not the underlying cause of this documented primary aldosteronism.

subject: Medicine
topic: Primary Biliary Cholangitis First-Line Ursodeoxycholic Acid Therapy
stem: A 51-year-old woman presents to the clinic with persistent generalized pruritus that is most intense on the palms and soles and worse at night. She also reports progressive daytime fatigue for the past 6 months. She has no abdominal pain, dark urine, acholic stools, or history of alcohol use. Her medical history includes Hashimoto thyroiditis treated with levothyroxine. On physical examination, skin examination reveals excoriations across both arms and legs, along with subtle yellowish planar xanthomas on her inner eyelids (xanthelasma). There is no jaundice, scleral icterus, spider angiomas, or ascites. Laboratory studies demonstrate: serum alkaline phosphatase 410 U/L (normal 30-120 U/L), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) 185 U/L (normal < 40 U/L), ALT 58 U/L, AST 52 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, and serum albumin 4.1 g/dL. Serum antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) titer is strongly positive at 1:320 (normal < 1:20). Total cholesterol is 280 mg/dL with HDL 78 mg/dL. Right upper quadrant abdominal ultrasound reveals normal liver echotexture, no intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation, and no gallstones. In accordance with AASLD and EASL clinical practice guidelines, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Perform a percutaneous core liver biopsy prior to initiating any pharmacotherapy
options.explanation: Liver biopsy is not necessary to establish the diagnosis of PBC when both chronic cholestatic liver enzymes and positive high-titer AMA (>= 1:40) are present, and would delay effective therapy.

options.text: Perform endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) to evaluate for ductal strictures
options.explanation: ERCP is invasive and indicated for large-duct biliary disease such as primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC); PBC affects microscopic interlobular ducts that are not visualized on ERCP.

options.text: Initiate high-dose oral prednisone 40 mg daily to suppress autoimmune cholangitis
options.explanation: Systemic corticosteroids are ineffective in halting PBC disease progression, cause accelerated severe osteoporosis in postmenopausal women with chronic cholestasis, and are contraindicated.

options.text: Initiate oral ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) at a weight-based dose of 13 to 15 mg/kg/day, monitoring liver biochemical tests every 3 to 6 months
options.explanation: This patient presents with classic PRIMARY BILIARY CHOLANGITIS (PBC, formerly primary biliary cirrhosis), an autoimmune cholestatic liver disease characterized by T-lymphocyte-mediated progressive destruction of small intrahepatic interlobular bile ducts. Per AASLD and EASL guidelines, the diagnosis of PBC is established when AT LEAST TWO OF THREE CRITERIA are met: (1) Biochemical evidence of cholestasis (predominantly elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT); (2) Presence of circulating ANTIMITOCHONDRIAL ANTIBODIES (AMA titer >= 1:40; present in > 95% of patients); and (3) Histopathologic evidence of non-suppurative destructive cholangitis on liver biopsy. Because the patient meets criteria 1 and 2, and extrahepatic biliary obstruction is excluded by normal ultrasound, LIVER BIOPSY IS NOT REQUIRED for diagnosis. The FIRST-LINE DISEASE-MODIFYING THERAPY IS URSODEOXYCHOLIC ACID (UDCA) at a weight-based dose of 13 TO 15 MG/KG/DAY. UDCA replaces hydrophobic, cytotoxic endogenous bile salts with hydrophilic, cytoprotective ursodiol, stimulates biliary bicarbonate secretion ('bicarbonate umbrella'), and inhibits cholangiocyte apoptosis. High-quality trial data prove that UDCA slows histological disease progression, improves transplant-free survival, and delays the need for liver transplantation.

options.text: Initiate oral cholestyramine 4 g three times daily as sole primary disease-modifying therapy
options.explanation: Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant that alleviates pruritus symptoms by binding intestinal bile salts, but it has zero disease-modifying effect and does not slow PBC liver disease progression.

subject: Medicine
topic: HLA-B*5801 Genetic Screening and Pharmacogenomics Prior to Allopurinol
stem: A 56-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry presents to the rheumatology clinic for management of recurrent polyarticular gout. Over the past 2 years, he has suffered four acute flares involving his right great toe, left midfoot, and right knee, confirmed by synovial fluid polarized microscopy demonstrating intracellular negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. His past medical history includes stage 3b chronic kidney disease (baseline serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, estimated GFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m2) and hypertension. His current medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily and losartan 50 mg daily. On examination, he has palpable subcutaneous tophi on the helix of his right ear and overlying the right olecranon. Laboratory evaluation reveals serum urate 9.6 mg/dL. He has had no previous exposure to allopurinol or febuxostat. In accordance with American College of Rheumatology (ACR) guidelines and the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC), which of the following actions is mandatory prior to initiating allopurinol therapy in this patient?

options.text: Perform pharmacogenetic testing for the HLA-B*5701 allele; if negative, allopurinol may be safely initiated at standard doses
options.explanation: HLA-B*5701 testing is mandatory prior to initiating ABACAVIR in HIV-infected patients to prevent severe abacavir hypersensitivity reaction; it has no relationship to allopurinol.

options.text: Initiate allopurinol 300 mg daily immediately without genetic testing, as CKD stage 3b accelerates allopurinol hepatic clearance
options.explanation: CKD impairs clearance of the active metabolite oxypurinol, increasing—not decreasing—hypersensitivity risk; starting allopurinol at 300 mg without HLA testing in a Han Chinese patient with CKD is dangerous.

options.text: Perform pharmacogenetic testing for the CYP2C19*2 loss-of-function allele prior to allopurinol prescription
options.explanation: CYP2C19 testing is used to evaluate clopidogrel responsiveness; allopurinol is metabolized by xanthine oxidase and aldehyde oxidase, not CYP2C19.

options.text: Perform glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency screening before allopurinol therapy
options.explanation: G6PD screening is mandatory prior to rasburicase or pegloticase (recombinant uricases that generate hydrogen peroxide and cause methemoglobinemia/hemolysis in G6PD deficiency), but is not required for allopurinol.

options.text: Perform pharmacogenetic testing for the HLA-B*5801 allele; if positive, allopurinol is contraindicated and an alternative agent (such as febuxostat) should be selected
options.explanation: ALLOPURINOL is the first-line urate-lowering therapy for gout, but it carries a severe, life-threatening risk of ALLOPURINOL HYPERSENSITIVITY SYNDROME (AHS) / SEVERE CUTANEOUS ADVERSE REACTIONS (SCAR), including STEVENS-JOHNSON SYNDROME (SJS) and TOXIC EPIDERMAL NECROLYSIS (TEN), which carry mortality rates up to 25-30%. The development of AHS/SCAR is extraordinarily strongly associated with the HLA-B*5801 ALLELE (odds ratio > 500 in Southeast Asians). Per ACR and CPIC guidelines, PHARMACOGENETIC TESTING FOR HLA-B*5801 IS CONDITIONALLY RECOMMENDED PRIOR TO INITIATING ALLOPURINOL in patients of SUBPOPULATIONS WITH HIGH ALLELE PREVALENCE: individuals of SOUTHEAST ASIAN DESCENT (Han Chinese, Korean, Thai; allele frequency 6-8%) and AFRICAN AMERICAN PATIENTS (allele frequency ~4%). Furthermore, concurrent CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE is a major synergistic risk factor for allopurinol-induced SCAR. If the patient tests POSITIVE for HLA-B*5801, ALLOPURINOL IS STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED; FEBUXOSTAT (a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor) is the recommended alternative agent.
